children: Based on where retail investors bought Nvidia shares on the dip last week, their gains are now nearly all gone, according to Vanda Research
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reacts to an ovation from employees upon his return to the company's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.
Shares of Nvidia fell for a second straight day on Wednesday, despite cheers from employees on Tuesday as Jensen Huang returned to the helm as CEO.
While Nvidia's stock (NVDA) skyrocketed 31.5% on Monday, 40% of those gains have now been erased as investors digest what Huang's return actually means for the stock.

"The 'half-life' of the 'Trump put' that was triggered by Huang's reinstatement seems to be rather short," Interactive Brokers strategist Steve Sosnick told MarketWatch. The fact that Huang was reinstated with President Trump's backing led some to believe Trump would continue to take steps to reverse the selloff in the stock, according to Sosnick - but that confidence might be short-lived.
He said it was natural to expect some profit-taking after Monday's dramatic surge for the stock, and added that Wednesday's decline "seems to be part of a broader trend toward risk-off."
Shares of Nvidia closed 3.9% lower at $149.30 on Wednesday, after dropping 5.9% on Tuesday. At current prices, the shares have lost $15.75 since Monday, or 40% of the $39.52 gain seen on Monday.

Iskandar Rakhmatov, a portfolio manager at quantitative-strategy research platform Zeus Quanto, told MarketWatch that the drop in Nvidia's stock Wednesday was expected, but that the landscape for retail investors is shifting.

"Buying the dip in Nvidia has worked for years, and it may work again. But the risks now go beyond chip demand: governance, politics and how the growth is financed," he said, referring to some of the key challenges facing Nvidia despite Huang's return as CEO.

According to a report from Vanda Research, retail investors paid roughly $148 a share on average for Nvidia's stock last week. The Wednesday close of $149.30 a share suggests most of those investors' gains have evaporated if they had yet to sell.
"Many who bought earlier in the month are still underwater," Rakhmatov said.

He added that, for most retail investors, "the real issue is position size," noting that many people own the stock directly as well as through index funds. "This is when concentration risk materializes," Rakhmatov said.
"There's a lot of emotion around Nvidia, so it's going to trade wild," Elazar Advisors analyst Chaim Siegel told MarketWatch, referring to the stock's selloff on Friday and its Monday reversal.

Another bad sign for Nvidia is the fact that Anthropic (ANT) broke below its IPO price, which Siegel described as a "spook to the AI story." That's further added to concerns around support for the artificial-intelligence trade and confidence in "where companies are going to get money to buy Nvidia chips."
